chapters.html:
It had been too long.

Phainon hadn’t been counting, but the weight of Mydei’s absence had carved itself into the spaces between his ribs, like an ache he never quite got used to. Kremnos was his duty now, its battlefields his eternal burden, and Okhema—no, Phainon—was never meant to see him again. That was the truth. And yet, Mydei was here.

The moment Phainon heard the news, he had bolted toward the great hall, barely keeping his composure. He thought he’d be met with something dramatic—something befitting their reunion. Maybe Mydei standing in the moonlight, half-shadowed, exuding quiet melancholy. Maybe he’d turn at the sound of Phainon’s voice, their eyes meeting with the weight of all that had been lost.

Instead, Phainon skidded to a stop in the doorway and found Mydei deep in discussion with Aglaea.

His arrival went entirely unnoticed.

“—The tides are unpredictable,” Mydei was saying, his tone steady, eyes focused. “Nikador’s flames burn through the corruption, yet they do not endure indefinitely. If Okhema is not fortified against the impending surge —”

“We must not be complacent,” Aglaea interjected, her voice smooth but carrying an edge. “Every moment we delay invites catastrophe. Time is not our ally in this, Mydei.”

Phainon should have been listening. He should have cared.

Instead, Mydei’s presence hit him like a goddamn chariot.

Phainon had always thought Mydei carried himself well, but this—this was something else. A quiet, immovable regality settled in his posture, in the way he stood, arms crossed, weight balanced with thoughtless precision.

His voice had the same strength it always had, but it was smoother, deeper in a way that settled into Phainon’s bones.

And the air around him—the sheer weight of it.

There was no physical change, no sudden increase in stature, but he felt bigger. Like space yielded to him, like his mere existence commanded attention. The divinity in him wasn’t loud or ostentatious, but undeniable.

Phainon swallowed. Hard.

No. This was not the time.

He forced himself to focus, stepping forward, arms crossed in what he hoped was a casual gesture. “If we already know the tides are unpredictable,” he cut in, “shouldn’t we be planning for worst-case scenarios instead of talking about time we might not have?”

Both Mydei and Aglaea turned to him. Mydei’s gaze was unreadable. Aglaea’s was infuriatingly knowing.

Phainon opened his mouth, ready to double down, to prove that he was still a functioning person and not three seconds away from eating Mydei alive.

And then Mydei raised a single eyebrow.

Shit.

It was barely anything. A small shift, a flicker of curiosity, as if Mydei had caught the way Phainon’s pulse skyrocketed and was mulling over whether or not to acknowledge it.

Aglaea didn’t have to mull over anything. Her expression screamed I know exactly what’s going on in that perverted little head of yours.

Phainon desperately tried to act normal. “What?”

“Nothing,” Mydei said, tone neutral, before turning back to Aglaea. Ignoring him.

Aglaea followed suit, her voice perfectly even as she continued, “Then we must reinforce our defenses to withstand the inevitable onslaught. The Black Tide will not wait for our preparations.”

Phainon, humiliated beyond repair, wanted to fling himself out the nearest window.

Then, as if to fully end his suffering, Castorice—quiet, serious, usually unbothered Castorice—glanced at him and gave him a sympathetic look.

No. Absolutely not. He could not live like this.

He could not survive like this.

Phainon, wisely, chose silence.

Not that he’d ever admit it.

He wasn’t sulking. He wasn’t. He was merely… observing. Like a strategist. Like someone who had tact and self-control and wasn’t just sitting there like a scolded child while Mydei and Aglaea continued their conversation, completely undisturbed by his suffering.

Fine. Whatever. He didn’t care.

He focused on Mydei instead.

It was easier now, without those sharp gazes pressing down on him. To just —look.

Small things had changed. Subtle. His presence had always been heavy, but now it was something else entirely—something vast, something commanding. Mydei had always carried himself with confidence, but this was different. It wasn’t learned. It wasn’t forced. It was just there, as if the world itself had yielded to him and he had accepted it without question.

It should have been unsettling. But it wasn’t.

Because for every change, there was something that remained achingly the same.

The tilt of his head when he listened intently. The way he still furrowed his brows when something actually required his attention. That sharp, assessing gaze that had always seen through everything.

Mydei was still Mydei. The same prince Phainon had fallen in love with.

Phainon swallowed around the feeling that thought brought.

And then—unfortunately—he kept thinking.

Because, oh no.

This Mydei, the one standing there with all the weight of divinity behind him, was still the same man Phainon had fucked into mattresses in the past.

And now, that thought was very dangerous.

It had been competitive, once. A clash of egos as much as bodies. Mydei could be stubborn as hell in all things, including sex, and Phainon had never backed down from a challenge. He remembered the way Mydei’s breath had hitched when he’d been the one leading, the way his nails had dug into Phainon’s back, the flickers of rare, open vulnerability that Phainon had earned with gritted teeth and sheer willpower.

Could he—

Would he—

Could he make this Mydei look like that?

His thoughts started spiraling.

Would Mydei’s voice still shake just a little if Phainon—No.

Would his fingers still grasp at Phainon’s arms if he pushed him deep enough—No. No, no.

Would he still make those same sounds if—

Absolutely not.

Phainon forcibly stopped his thoughts before they derailed into actual insanity. He inhaled sharply through his nose, gritted his teeth, and thought of anything else.

There was absolutely no way in hell he was going to sit here, listening to a serious conversation about the fate of Okhema, while getting turned on like some kind of depraved idiot.

He was fine.

Everything was fine.

He just needed to breathe. And not think about anything.

…This was going to be a long night.

He had waited. He had suffered. He had sat there, like some kind of forsaken saint, through the entirety of Mydei and Aglaea’s conversation without embarrassing himself further. And now—

Now.

Mydei was finally going to acknowledge him.

A long-awaited reunion.

Except—

…Mydei walked right past him.

Phainon blinked.

Once.

Twice.

What.

He turned his head just in time to see the trailing edge of Mydei’s clothes as he strode away. Not a word, not a glance—just leaving, as if Phainon wasn’t even there.

His stomach dropped. By the time he could talk again, Mydei was already out on the streets, about to take his leave.

“Mydei—wait.”

His voice wasn’t loud, but it carried.

And Mydei—

Stopped.

Phainon nearly tripped over his own feet.

Because Mydei actually stopped. He sighed, turning just enough to glance at Phainon over his shoulder—his expression unreadable, his golden eyes half-lidded, expectant.

Waiting.

And Phainon… did not know what to do with that.

He hadn’t expected Mydei to actually listen.

Not after all this time. Not after—everything.

The air between them sat heavy as Phainon caught up, stopping just within arm’s reach. Up close, the weight of Mydei’s presence was even worse. It pressed against the skin, seeped into the lungs, coiled deep in the gut with an unbearable mix of emotions Phainon hadn’t had time to sort through.

So, naturally, he panicked.

“The Black Tide,” he blurted out, desperate for something, anything to ground him. “How—how are things at Castrum Kremnos?”

Mydei didn’t answer immediately. His gaze flickered—briefly, imperceptibly—to Phainon’s throat, where his pulse betrayed him. Then, in that same measured, deliberate voice, he said:

“Manageable.”

Phainon had no idea why that single word felt like it shook the world a little.

Maybe it was the way Mydei said it. The quiet, absolute certainty in his tone. Like the Black Tide—an apocalyptic force—was nothing more than an inevitability to be faced and conquered.

There was no arrogance in it.

Just Fact.

Phainon should have left it at that. Should have pressed for more details, anything to prolong the conversation. Instead, he kept looking.

And the longer he looked, the worse it got.

Mydei had always been beautiful. Regal. Unwavering. But this—

This was different.

There was something lethal about the ease with which he held himself now. Like a blade no longer unsheathed in defiance, but simply worn—an extension of himself, honed to perfection. The weight of his divinity was suffocatingly severe, and that should have been terrifying.

It wasn’t.

It was doing something else to Phainon entirely.

Because damn.

His presence alone had already been overwhelming, but now all of that power was wrapped in Mydei’s voice, Mydei’s face, Mydei’s hands—

This was beyond what he was prepared for.

Phainon had always had a thing for strong people. He was not built to handle this.

He needed to pull himself together immediately.

His mouth opened—to say something, to salvage what little remained of his dignity—

And then he heard the gasp.

“The King of Kremnos!”

Phainon barely had time to blink before the first child ran up, eyes impossibly wide, staring up at Mydei in absolute awe.

And then—more.

A few more voices, scattered murmurs. Hardened Kremnoans—warriors, survivors—began to take notice, gathering at the edges of the market. Watching. Waiting.

Phainon turned back, half-expecting Mydei to ignore it. To move on, like he was detached.

But Mydei… paused.

He turned slightly, golden gaze lowering to meet the child’s. The flicker of recognition, the briefest shift in his expression—softer.

Gentler.

Phainon knew Mydei. He knew how he held himself—sharp-edged and resolute before men who had once called him prince, before people who had long since learned to carve their place in the world with steel.

But with children—

With Kremnoan children, who had already lost too much—

He softened. Just enough.

The child stepped closer, tiny hands gripping the edge of Mydei’s clothesas if making sure he was real.

“You came back.”

A heartbeat of silence.

Mydei knelt.

And smiled.

Phainon’s brain ceased all function.

He was so fucked.

He needed to breathe. He needed to turn away before—

A firm grip found his waist. Oh yeah, he was in front of Mydei, wasn’t he? Blocking his way.

Phainon’s soul left his body.

He barely had time to process it before he was being moved, the hands guiding Phainon’s slow feet as his brain struggled to catch up.

Effortlessly.

Casually.

One moment, he was standing right in front of Mydei, still in the process of comprehending the sheer depth of his own depravity, and the next—

He was somewhere else.

Because Mydei, without hesitation, without even breaking his stride, had simply placed a hand on Phainon’s waist and moved him aside. Like furniture.

Phainon blacked out for a second.

Not literally. But spiritually.

His entire soul went static.

This was bad.

There was no ceremony to it. No dramatics. Just Mydei touching him like it was nothing, Mydei using all that strength effortlessly, Mydei moving him like some inconvenient object—

Phainon needed to lie down immediately.

But he couldn’t. Because he was still standing there, frozen, in the middle of the street, surrounded by people.

This was fine.

He was fine.

Everything was completely, absolutely fine.

…Right?

Okay no, Phainon actually needed to lie down.

Like, immediately.

It wasn’t a metaphor, it wasn’t an exaggeration—his knees were about to give out.

He moved. Automatically. Head down, eyes fixed on the cobblestones, hands clenched so tightly he could feel his nails biting into his palms. He barely heard the voices around him—Kremnoan warriors murmuring, children whispering in awe, the steady, calm cadence of Mydei’s voice as he answered them.

Phainon walked.

Nowhere in particular, just away. A quiet, unremarkable exit before he embarrassed himself any further.

Somehow, miraculously, he made it to a stone bench. He sat.

And then—

He pressed both hands to his face and exhaled through his nose so hard he nearly saw stars.

He was going insane.

That was the only explanation.

Because what the fuck was that?

Mydei had barely touched him. It had been so casual. And yet Phainon was sitting here, fists clenched in his lap, body overwhelmingly aware of every single place Mydei’s fingers had been.

He wanted to scream.

Not from frustration. Not from embarrassment.

From need.

He wanted to ruin him.

He wanted to drag Mydei into the nearest secluded space and mark him up. Kiss him, bite him, press him against the nearest surface and see if he could still make him shudder like before. If this new, untouchable, divine Mydei could still fall apart in his hands.

Gods.

He needed to stop thinking about this.

Right now.

Phainon forced himself to sit up. To breathe.

To get a fucking grip.

Because he was in public.

And Mydei—Mydei was literally right there.

And Phainon—

Needed to leave the vicinity.

He should have just stood up and walked away. Left the marketplace, locked himself in a room somewhere, and prayed for deliverance.

But no. He sat there.

Watching.

It wasn’t his fault. It wasn’t.

Because Mydei—King of Kremnos, God of Strife, Destroyer of Phainon’s Sanity—was standing there, completely at ease among his people, answering their questions with that same measured calm he always had.

But it was different now.

Not because his voice was deeper, not because he looked any different. No, Mydei was still the same prince Phainon had known, still the same man he had fought beside, bled beside—fucked senseless into his own bedsheets.

But the presence.

That was what made Phainon’s throat go dry.

It was an undeniable weight. Something in the way Mydei carried himself now—unshaken, unmovable, absolute.

And he was so damn good with children.

A little girl, barely past his knee, hesitated before reaching for his hand. And Mydei let her. Lowered himself slightly so that their heights weren’t so different, listened carefully as she mumbled something Phainon couldn’t hear.

A man who could shatter mountains with a touch, bowing his head to a child.

Something in Phainon’s brain short-circuited.

Sweet Kephale.

There was no coming back from this.

If he didn’t leave now, he was going to do something stupid.

So he forced himself to stand.

Took one last look at Mydei, then turned away before the hunger clawing up his spine made him ruin his own reputation.

And then—

“Leaving so soon?”

Phainon froze.

He turned slowly, carefully schooling his expression, only to meet Mydei’s gaze.

And that was worse.

Because Mydei was looking at him like he was the strange one, like he was some puzzle to be solved.

“I—” Phainon’s mouth went dry. “Just needed a moment.”

A long moment. Preferably several hours. Somewhere very far away.

“If you have something to say, say it.”

“Who says I have anything to say?” Phainon forced a smirk, leaning back slightly, trying to regain some semblance of control.

Mydei didn’t even blink.

“You’re staring again.”

Phainon nearly choked.

He tried to cover it with a scoff. “Yeah? Maybe you’re just nice to look at.”

There. Counterattack.

A hit, clean and smooth.

Except—

Nothing.

Not a smirk, not a raised brow.

Nothing.

Just a slight shift in Mydei’s expression—something too mild, too composed.

“Did I do something to offend?”

And that was it. That was what broke him.

Because how was he supposed to deal with this?

With this Mydei—this new Mydei—who said things like that so seriously?

Phainon clenched his teeth so hard it hurt.

He couldn’t even fight back. Not like before, not like when it had been a game between them. Because how the hell was he supposed to make Mydei flustered now?

How did you fluster a god?

There was only one way to find out.

Phainon wasn’t about to let himself be thrown off twice.

The initial shock had been one thing, but he had pride. He had survived wars, gods, and disasters of world-ending proportions. He refused to be undone by something as simple as Mydei existing too well.

So he pulled himself together and leaned into the conversation like it was effortless.

“Offend me?” he repeated smoothly, tilting his head with a smirk. “Mydei, if you ever managed to offend me, I’d be worried for your health.”

A small exhale, almost a laugh, and just like that—the rhythm was back.

God or not, Mydei was still Mydei. Still sharp, still composed, still a man of measured responses and infuriating calm.

And Phainon knew exactly how to press his buttons.

Their conversation shifted like a dance—familiar steps, well-worn patterns. Mydei was direct, clipped in his responses, while Phainon was all smooth deflections and teasing remarks, dodging around serious topics with ease.

It was easy. It was natural.

And yet, somewhere along the way, Phainon found himself watching too closely.

Noticing things he hadn’t had the chance to before.

The way Mydei spoke now—not just as a warrior, but as a man who carried a kingdom on his back. The way his gestures had grown more restrained, his every movement deliberate, as if he had learned the weight of a single glance.

But then—

The slight furrow of his brow when he disagreed with something. The near-invisible shift in his expression when he was actually amused. The quiet patience in the way he listened, even when someone was being ridiculous.

Some things hadn’t changed at all.

And Phainon—helplessly, irreversibly—felt himself soften.

His lips quirked slightly, his gaze lingering longer than he meant for it to.

“Stop looking at me like that.”

The words came low, even, but the averted gaze gave him away.

Phainon stilled. “Like what?”

A pause.

And in that silence, realization slammed into him.

Oh.

Oh.

This was new.

For the first time since Mydei had returned—since he had become a god— Phainon had found something real.

A crack in the armor.

Something warm and human beneath the impossible, unshaken composure.

And he was going to enjoy this.

Phainon took a slow breath, schooling his expression into something smooth, composed, entirely in control.

“You’re going to have to be more specific,” he said, tilting his head with a lazy smile. “I look at you in a lot of ways.”

Mydei’s gaze flicked back to him, cool and unreadable. “And this one?”

Phainon hummed, pretending to consider it. “Hmm. If I had to name it, I’d say… admiration.”

A dry look. “Admiration.”

Phainon grinned. “Is that so hard to believe? I mean, here you are—ruler of Kremnos, commander of the front, savior of your people. And still— somehow—not the least bit unapproachable. It’s almost unfair, really.”

Mydei raised a brow. “Unfair?”

Phainon leaned in slightly. Just a fraction. Enough to make it noticeable. Enough to see if Mydei would react.

“It’s just a little overwhelming,” he continued, voice dropping just a touch lower. “The whole package, I mean. Strong, noble, unwavering. And then I see you with those kids earlier, and—” he let out a slow breath, shaking his head with a knowing look. “Mydei, you’re making it difficult for me.”

There. A hit.

Mydei’s fingers twitched slightly at his side—a movement so minuscule, so insignificant, that anyone else would have missed it.

But Phainon didn’t.

He pressed forward, voice dipping into something warmer, slower. “Tell me, do you even know what you do to people when you—”

“Phainon.”

It wasn’t sharp.

Not a warning, not a dismissal, just his name.

And before Phainon could even process it, Mydei reached out—barely moving, barely even trying—and rested a hand against his shoulder.

Not firm. Not rough. Just enough.

Just enough for Phainon’s brain to completely, utterly, and catastrophically shut down.

Because how was this fair?

How was he supposed to deal with someone who was this?

Mydei—who was already so many things, too many things—was also calm, collected, untouchable. Strong enough to effortlessly throw Phainon off balance, composed enough to make it seem like he hadn’t even noticed what he was doing.

And it wasn’t even arrogance.

It wasn’t even conscious. That was the worst part.

He was just like this.

Phainon had no choice but to spiral again.

And then—just as Phainon was barely managing to piece himself back together—

Mydei squeezed his shoulder.

Just briefly. Just enough for warmth to linger.

Then, effortlessly, devastatingly—

“Behave.”

The word echoed in his skull.

Behave.

His body had betrayed him first, a full-body shiver he could do nothing to suppress. Then his mind followed, spiraling so bad he couldn’t even form words.

For the first time in a long time, Phainon had no response.

The seconds stretched.

Mydei—unaffected—waited.

Phainon could feel his eyes on him, expectant at first, then slightly amused. The patience of a man who could hold a battlefield for eternity, waiting for Phainon to put himself back together.

Except he couldn’t.

After a full minute of silence, Mydei seemed to take it as defeat.

Without a word, he shifted—turning away, ready to leave.

Phainon felt something in him snap.

Oh, no. No, no, no.

He’d barely survived this encounter as it was—if Mydei walked away now, with this last image of him, he’d never recover.

Dignity be damned.

Phainon lurched forward.

Just before Mydei could take his first step, he caught his wrist.

Or—at least, he tried.

Mydei moved faster, catching Phainon’s forearm before he could grab his own, fingers wrapping around him with frustrating ease.

It was effortless. Everything was so effortless for him now.

Phainon barely had time to process it before Mydei sighed.

A small, nearly exasperated sound.

Then—without any fanfare, without even asking, Mydei pulled him along.

Not forcefully, though. Just enough to make it clear Phainon wasn’t getting left behind.

And Phainon—humiliated, reeling, hopelessly turned on—could do nothing but follow.

Phainon was still recovering.

He had, in the span of minutes, been shut down, rendered speechless, and manhandled like some helpless maiden in a tragic love ballad. And now he was being dragged through Okhema’s streets, hand locked in Mydei’s grip, like a scolded child.

It should have been humiliating.

It was humiliating.

And yet—

Mydei’s hand was warm. Steady. Familiar.

Phainon let himself be led for a while, gaze lingering on the way Mydei’s fingers curled so easily around his own. He flexed his hand slightly, testing the hold. Mydei didn’t react, didn’t let go—just adjusted his grip, absentmindedly intertwining their fingers.

Phainon swallowed. “So we’re holding hands now.”

Mydei didn’t even glance at him. “You grabbed me first.”

Phainon scoffed. “I was trying to stop you from leaving, not—” he gestured vaguely at their hands, “—whatever this is.”

“You’re complaining?”

Phainon huffed. “Would it kill you to at least pretend to be flustered?”

Mydei finally glanced at him, expression dry. “You’d like that, wouldn’t you?”

Phainon grinned. “Obviously.”

A beat of silence.

Then, to his utter shock, Mydei gave his hand a small, deliberate squeeze.

Phainon almost choked.

He turned to Mydei so fast it was a miracle he didn’t give himself whiplash. “Was that—did you just—was that affectionate?”

Mydei exhaled through his nose, something almost like a laugh. “You really are hopeless.”

Phainon beamed. “And yet, here you are, still holding my hand.”

Mydei didn’t let go.

Didn’t even try.

Phainon’s heart did something stupid and ridiculous.

And for once, he let it.

By the time they found themselves somewhere secluded—a quiet, dimly lit space tucked away from the city’s bustling streets—Phainon had fully convinced himself that this time, he had the upper hand.

It was ridiculous, really. Embarrassing, even. But he needed one victory tonight. Just one.

So when Mydei finally stopped, looking at him expectantly, Phainon didn’t hesitate.

He stepped in, close enough that their bodies almost touched. He tilted Mydei’s chin up, a slow, deliberate motion, letting his fingers linger at the sharp edge of his jaw.

Smirk in place, voice dropping low, he murmured, “What would you do if I —”

His back hit the nearest surface before he even finished the sentence.

Phainon blinked.

What.

Mydei had moved so fast, that Phainon barely had time to process it before he found himself pinned.

One of Mydei’s hands pressed firm against his chest, keeping him in place. The other—Saints above, when had he even grabbed Phainon’s wrist?— held his arm up, restrained like it was nothing.

Phainon’s brain short-circuited.

Oh, no.

Oh, no.

He was actually going to die.

Mydei tilted his head slightly, expression calm, composed, completely unaffected. Like he hadn’t just effortlessly put Phainon exactly where he wanted him.

“I’d do this,” Mydei said simply.

Phainon swallowed hard.

Saints save him.

Phainon, still pinned, still barely processing his situation, stared up at Mydei with wide eyes.

Then, finally, he managed to gather what little dignity he had left.

“So,” he started, voice only slightly strained, “I’m going to assume that means you’re interested.”

Mydei gave him a look. “No.”

Phainon’s stomach plummeted.

“What—”

“Not here.”

Oh.

Phainon exhaled, the tension in his chest loosening—only for a new kind of suffering to replace it.

Because not here didn’t mean no.

It just meant he had to wait.

Phainon tried not to let his desperation show. “You didn’t have an issue last time.”

Mydei’s expression didn’t change. “You’re questioning my standards?”

“I’m questioning why you suddenly have them.”

Mydei raised a brow.

Phainon scowled. “Fine. Fine. We’ll do things your way.”

The second Mydei let him go, Phainon immediately turned away—so he wouldn’t embarrass himself by visibly shaking.

He ran a hand through his hair, exhaling hard, forcing himself to think about something—anything—that would keep him from losing it completely.

He barely lasted five minutes before realizing he was actually suffering.

And judging by the way Mydei was watching him now, clearly amused, he knew it.

Bastard.

The moment the door closed behind them, Phainon was on him.

He didn’t hesitate—not this time.

He surged forward, grabbing Mydei by the waist, backing him up until the backs of his legs hit the bed.

And then—with all the confidence of a man who hadn’t just been pinned a minute ago—Phainon pushed him down.

Mydei let it happen.

Which was the first sign that something was terribly, terribly wrong.

Phainon was too caught up in his own victory to notice.

He climbed over him, smirk sharp, hands braced at either side of Mydei’s waist.

“Now,” he murmured, leaning in, letting his breath ghost over Mydei’s lips. “Where were we?”

For half a second, Mydei actually humored him.

He stayed there, flat on his back, looking up at Phainon with something unreadable in his gaze.

Phainon felt it—the shift, the thrill and satisfaction of finally having Mydei beneath him.

He was winning.

And then—
